detail.heading: The eight decisions
items: 1. Booking, press and partner inbox plus phone, and who owns the replies.
2. Coach's current fee range and existing agreements (speaking bureaus, Hachette, Paramount, likeness).
3. Footage position: license the film scenes, host them privately, or use official embeds only.
4. The two lead offers (likely candidates: the Contract team pilot plus keynotes, or a sponsored Academy season).
5. Academy series concept: Coach as a player (the current site) vs next-generation students (the playbook's recommendation: no lesson that only works because Coach appears).
6. Real headshots and recent footage of Coach speaking, plus his own quotes in his own words.
7. Foundation / Coach Carter Impact Academy legal status, and a trademark search on "Coach Carter Academy".
8. Which tools to pay for (CRM, email platform, Stripe or Shopify, video hosting, data room). The playbook budgets $8K for web, CRM and analytics inside the $60K test.

detail.heading: The ten biggest blind spots, most costly first
items: 1. Every lead is lost: inquiry forms save to the visitor's own browser, and email forms reset and discard.
2. No way to reach a human: no email or phone anywhere on the site.
3. No way to pay: the cart says the store opens soon; books in print aren't linked to retailers.
4. No owned audience: no email list or analytics. The playbook calls the owned list the asset that changes the valuation.
5. Trust gaps: AI images of Coach shown without a label; film lines credited to Coach instead of the 2005 film; no footage of Coach speaking after 2015.
6. Legal and rights exposure: no legal pages; film scenes public; "Coach Carter Academy" vs the real Coach Carter Impact Academy; no trademark search.
7. Too many offers: 10 plays plus 5 pilots on show; the playbook says sell two first.
8. No back office: no pipeline, proposals, contracts, invoicing or calendar that protects Coach's hours.
9. Strategy drift: the series logline (Coach returns as a player) differs from the playbook's Academy (next-generation students).
10. No named team: no booking desk, press lead or facilitator named; testimonials mostly undated; no current outcomes.

sections.title: The playbook in one page
sections.why_left_out: The site turned this into sales copy; the honest caveats ("unestablished", "not a verified market rate") were dropped.
key_points: The goal is a lasting global franchise built around the brand, not Coach's personal net worth.
Verdict: pursue it seriously, but no public evidence sets today's value or the odds of reaching $500M or $1B.
Today's brand value is "Unestablished": no authenticated financials, audience data or Carter deal supports a number.
A first sale is assumed at $75K with $55K direct cost, leaving $20K — neither is a verified market rate; get bids.
Lead with the Academy, use the documentary as a launch asset, and make the next step a paid proof.
All unsourced prices, costs, margins, royalties, multiples and sales targets are planning assumptions. No outreach or spending has happened.

detail.heading: The objective and the judgment
items: Objective: build the Coach Carter brand into a durable global franchise. The target is the brand and the business around it, rather than Coach's personal net worth.
Judgment: pursue this seriously. A recognizable story, a real founder, a clear code and a new Academy generation create a credible franchise opportunity.
A $500M or $1B outcome requires a large, repeatable commercial ecosystem. No public evidence establishes that valuation today or a reliable probability of reaching it.

detail.heading: The decisions to understand first (the playbook lists these under "six decisions"; seven bullets appear)
items: Lead with Academy. New students, parents, rivals and alumni can carry recurring stories. Coach supplies the standard; new characters make the world expandable.

Use the documentary as a major launch asset. The real man, present-day conflict and corroborated untold history give audiences another reason to care. A streamer is one possible buyer, alongside distributors, sponsors, screenings and publishing.
Sell entertainment with a business purpose. A brand can fund a story arc plus community activation. This is already happening in the market; Carter's actual price still needs a paid test.
Build beyond his calendar. Catalog licenses, local adaptations, partner clubs, useful products and character spin-offs can earn without Coach appearing personally every time.
Build the whole franchise. Stories, catalog, clubs, academies and consumer licenses create the commercial ecosystem. Value its earnings first; use standalone brand valuation as a component analysis.

Price the web series; give away only the preview. Proposed launch: $19.99 one-time Season One access. Full episodes behind paid access; the public site gets a separate 60-second preview. Checkout is not yet live.
Make the next decision a paid proof. Finish and assess the existing episode, sell a scoped continuation, reconcile delivered cost, and measure whether viewers and buyers return.

An alternative $300M mix cuts catalog receipts from $100M to $40M and includes $25M fully allocated network EBITDA: $540M–$735M sensitivity. Stronger margins in that mix produce $740M–$1.035B (details: chapter 14).

sections.title: The first 90 days, the $60K test and the four scale gates
sections.why_left_out: Internal budget, release conditions and sales targets — advice for Coach and Ralph, not a sales message.
key_points: $60,000 is a proposed planning cap, not authorization to spend; it excludes a full documentary or scripted season.
Money is released in three steps: up to $15K, then $20K, then $25K — each only after a gate is met.
Gate to the second step: three signed pilot orders with deposits collected, or a signed sponsor with first payment collected.
Interview 20 buyers in the first 30 days and sell no more than two offers first.
Free praise and nonbinding enthusiasm do not count; only booked, invoiced and collected money counts.
A $500M/$1B valuation conversation only becomes real at Gate 4, after durable growth and meaningful earnings.

detail.heading: Days 1–30: establish the baseline and sell (release up to $15,000)
items: Assemble financials, analytics, customer history, existing books/programs, and the current episode.
Interview 20 buyers: five brand/agency content buyers, five corporate workforce/community buyers, five school/youth buyers, and five sports/media buyers.
Compare three offers: the sponsored Academy package, the limited Coach-led video show, and a practical institutional program. Select no more than two to sell first.
Create the $19.99 planned season offer with a free 60-second preview; validate protected paid access before sales.
Record current Coach material, show the existing episode to target viewers, and request scoped production bids.
Test three Academy hook concepts and a coherent short arc; measure whether new characters retain viewers beyond recognition of Coach.

detail.heading: Gate 1 → release of the next tranche
items: Seek three signed pilot orders with deposits collected, or a signed sponsor commitment with an initial payment collected.
Track booked, invoiced, and collected amounts separately.
Free praise and nonbinding enthusiasm do not meet the gate.
If the offers fail, change the buyer, proposition, price, or delivery before increasing production spending.

detail.heading: Days 31–60: deliver and measure (release up to $20,000 after the gate)
items: Deliver the funded pilot: either a scoped content package with a production partner or a practical program with a qualified educator/facilitator.
For content, track completion, return viewing, distribution delivery, and the sponsor objective.
For programs, track participation, implementation, and buyer feedback.
Record direct costs and contribution for both.
Track baseline and follow-up without claiming that a small uncontrolled pilot proves causal academic improvement.
Assess the Academy cut and make a focused documentary treatment/proof plan.

detail.heading: Days 61–90: earn the next commitment (release up to $25,000 after delivery evidence)
items: Seek five total paid pilots and three speaking engagements; test actual offers and prices rather than assuming them.
Target: five $5,000 pilots plus three $15,000 speeches = $70,000 in gross bookings. It is a sales target, not promised revenue, collected cash, or profit.
In a sponsor-led path, deliver within the signed scope and seek a second season, renewal, or additional distribution partner.
Do not add the illustrative $75,000 package to the program-led bookings target as if both were certain.
Seek paid extensions and next-term commitments. Three of five buyers expressing renewal intent would be encouraging but is weaker evidence than actual paid renewal.
Scale recurring licenses after the first renewal cohort, not before.
Evaluate the present-day documentary proof and the strongest scripted concept with intended viewers and qualified buyers/operators.
Pursue one lead entertainment package with clear next steps. A full slate can remain on the opportunity board without being financed simultaneously.

Claude's five assets add to $605M–$1.45B, but they overlap; the same royalty can't be counted twice.
Platform equity ($25M–$100M) is the weakest line: count it as $0 until a signed, real stake exists.
$20M–$30M club profit needs $100M–$150M yearly company revenue; the brand can't replace a working youth-sports business.
Six participation properties and six first products are proposals, not tested prices — pick two for buyer interviews and a paid pilot.

detail.heading: Why the stack doesn't simply add up
items: The stated asset ranges add correctly to $605M–$1.45B, but do not mechanically follow every supplied endpoint: $40M × 18 = $720M while the IP row caps at $450M; $20M × 12 = $240M rather than the network's $250M floor; programs' endpoints imply $40M–$160M rather than $50M–$150M.
Applying all extreme endpoints yields $585M–$1.73B. Neither endpoint exercise is an appraisal. A selected, narrower range needs an explained valuation rationale.
Economic overlap: a character-product royalty cannot sit in both library licensing and consumer licensing. Club/program royalties cannot be valued again after they are in the network's earnings.
A subsidiary paying an internal brand royalty reduces its own profit; the group must eliminate internal transactions.
Each business needs its share of management, production, sales and support costs. Only independently attributable values can be combined, with ownership, debt and other claims reconciled.
Chapter 14's franchise-company and brand-asset cases remain alternatives, not extra amounts to place on this stack.

detail.heading: The weakest line: platform equity
items: Famous IP can be exchanged for cash plus warrants or equity, but Lionsgate/Runway or FOX/HOLYWATER deal structures do not establish that Carter can receive $25M–$100M of realizable stakes.
Seek a paid showcase or slate with a minimum cash commitment, a separately negotiated equity component and measurable distribution.
Count any eventual stake separately at evidenced value. Do not let speculative stock substitute for production cash.

detail.heading: The network's scale is the bigger operating challenge
items: $20M–$30M EBITDA at an assumed 20% margin requires $100M–$150M annual company revenue.
If Carter operates facilities, that entails delivery staff, venues and capital.
If the company instead earns a hypothetical 10% operator royalty, $100M–$150M fee revenue would require $1B–$1.5B of underlying operator sales, before considering different margins.
These are scale illustrations, not recommended prices. The brand can improve acquisition and retention; it cannot replace a working youth-sports business.

Claude's 5%/$1B and 10%/$500M figures are retained as its subjective seven-to-ten-year judgments, not calibrated probabilities. Update the investment case after contracts, retention, cash contribution and management capacity are demonstrated.

Don't claim: that those viewers have agreed to follow or buy from Coach.
Don't claim: "universally known" or "seen by everybody" — that is sales language, not established fact. No audited lifetime global audience or demographic recognition study was available.
To do: test recognition by country, age and buyer type.

His real advantage: an unknown creator must first explain why anyone should care; Coach starts with a recognizable cultural reference, a real person and a clear promise — education, accountability, belonging and performance.
How much that lowers marketing cost is still a test, not a measured fact.

sections.title: Three ways the company could look: small company, media studio, hybrid

key_points: These are imagined future years — not current results, forecasts or promises. No Carter sale supports the multiples used.
A lean speaking-and-programs business makes about $430K revenue and $64K profit; a scaled one, about $24M revenue and $4.8M profit.
Small education businesses sold at a median 2.22× (average 2.58×) owner earnings in 2021–2025 — so don’t borrow tech or media multiples.
A media-studio model: $17M revenue, $3.2M yearly operating profit, worth $25.6M-$38.4M on the assumed multiples.
The recommended direction is media-plus-programs toward $500M: $220M revenue, $62M profit — a scale target, not a forecast.
These models are alternatives — never add them together. First real proof: a distribution partner, repeat sponsor, library renewal and profitable delivery.

detail.heading: Ground rules
items: Illustrative future annual operating cases — not current results, probability-weighted forecasts, promises, or a ceiling on entertainment value.
No Carter transaction comparable supports the selected valuation multiples.
The first three cases exclude media; a separate media-led architecture follows. Chapter 20 includes the underlying unit inputs and formulas.
EBITDA = yearly operating profit (before interest, taxes and write-downs). EV (enterprise value) = what a buyer might pay for the whole company.

detail.heading: Case A: speaking + programs company (no media)
What those margins must pay for
items: Delivery staff, product development, sales, commissions, customer service, travel, insurance, marketing, technology, merchandise cost of goods, administration, and reasonable management compensation.
Coach cannot deliver every engagement and serve every school himself.
The institutional cases require hiring and working capital; customer counts are assumptions to be earned.

detail.heading: Reality check on the multiples
items: The multiples are selected sensitivity inputs, not verified Carter transaction multiples.
A small, founder-dependent speaking practice could trade on much less attractive terms.
At 3× EBITDA, the developed case would be about $1.46 million; the scaled case about $14.39 million.
A buyer may not exist at any modeled price.
BizBuySell’s reported 2021-2025 education/school sales: median 2.22× seller’s discretionary earnings, average 2.58×, and average 0.80× revenue [S30].

That is a broad small-business sample. Seller’s discretionary earnings are not EBITDA, and it is not a direct Coach Carter comparable — but it warns against casually applying media or technology multiples to a small education practice.

None of the project count, prices, margins or multiples were observed for Coach.
Production revenue can contain large pass-through costs; contribution and cash timing matter more than the headline budget.

This is an alternative, not a value to add to the institutional case. A combined business needs one consolidated P&L (profit-and-loss statement) with shared overhead, customer costs and overlapping revenue reconciled.
Consumer margins must include acquisition, fulfillment and refunds; licensing contribution must include residual delivery, sales and participation costs.
The high catalog margin depends heavily on the actual economic arrangements and a library built over time.

items: Multi-season commitments.
Repeat sponsor franchises.
An earning catalog.
International format partners.
An owned audience that reduces acquisition costs.
A capable operator.
Coach’s personal story opens the franchise; the company can later produce other compatible stories and talent — an expandable business, rather than every title retelling the same movie.

detail.heading: Case C: media-plus-programs route toward $500M (the recommended direction)
Case C notes
items: Called the stronger strategic direction for this team than leading with 20,000 school contracts: use Academy and the documentary to establish a production and distribution business; add repeat brand franchises, an earning library and partner-distributed programs; at scale, produce compatible stories beyond Coach personally.
It fits the team’s production capability and relationships better — but none of those capabilities establishes this revenue today.
A deliberately ambitious scale target — not a forecast or a sum to add to the other scenarios.
Less $30M central overhead (paid leadership, Coach compensation, development and audience infrastructure) → $62M EBITDA / 28.2% margin.
Selected 8-12× sensitivity → $496M-$744M EV.
At a lower 15% EBITDA margin and 8×, the same revenue gives $264M EV.
No Carter offer or observed multiple supports these assumed prices and values.
The $4M portfolios are multi-title/season packages at a future studio — not a quote for one Academy microdrama.

Campaigns exclude sponsorship already booked in production receipts. Catalog receipts exclude the same first-window fees. Each program contract counts once regardless of who underwrites it. Shared costs and affiliate transactions must reconcile in one P&L.

detail.heading: Which route needs fewer assumptions? Neither.
items: The media route needs fewer institutional accounts, but far larger media contracts, an accumulated earning library, international distribution and unusually strong margins.
It concentrates risk in a smaller number of buyers and needs working capital.
The 20,000-account route needs broad customer acquisition, implementation and retention.
Choose the media-led route for strategic fit; stage capital around commissions and renewals — not whichever story has the biggest spreadsheet.
First evidence that makes it more than arithmetic: a genuine first-look/distribution partner, a repeat sponsor, a successful library renewal and profitable delivery.

sections.title: The $500M and $1B targets: two franchise models
sections.why_left_out: Billion-dollar arithmetic is a destination with gates, not a valuation to publish today.
key_points: Two different things get valued: the whole franchise company, and the brand name itself. Never add them together.
Use the franchise company as the operating ambition; use the brand-asset number only for a narrow valuation claim.
A $300M-revenue franchise could be worth $680M-$1.02B — but only with $100M a year of high-profit catalog and license income.
A clubs-and-academies version cuts that catalog need 60% and still reaches $540M-$735M — $500M-plus, but not automatically $1B.
Reaching $1B with clubs needs much fatter margins across content, campaigns and programs — demanding and unproved.
Buying an existing profitable operator can speed things up, but its price, financing and dilution count — it isn’t free brand value.

Diversifying revenue does not automatically reproduce $1B.

detail.heading: Choose the network structure before quoting scale
items: At an illustrative 20% fully allocated EBITDA margin, $25M EBITDA requires $125M annual company revenue.
At an assumed 10% operator royalty and the same margin, that implies $1.25B of underlying operator sales.
A high-margin licensing network could need less company revenue; a facility-heavy network could need more capital.

Buying an existing profitable operator can accelerate the path, but the purchase price, financing, integration and ownership dilution must be included. Do not treat acquired earnings as free brand-created value.

sections.title: How a buyer would price the franchise — and the brand name alone
sections.why_left_out: Deal precedents and brand-royalty math are internal benchmarks, not Carter offers or comparables.
key_points: A buyer prices the whole franchise on expected future cash — characters, formats, catalog, licenses and growth — not on fame.
Peanuts sold at about 23× attributable earnings (C$630M for 41%) — proof premium franchises exist, not a price for Carter.
For a $1B brand name alone at a 5% royalty, licensees would need about $2.4B a year in branded sales.
Time matters: $1B ten years from now is worth only about $322M today at a 12% discount rate.
A billion-dollar company does not mean a billion-dollar trademark — the same $300M company gives a $125M brand value.
Verdict: keep the billion-dollar ambition, but today’s evidence only justifies pursuing the first proof — not a $500M or $1B valuation.

detail.heading: How a strategic buyer would value the franchise
items: Lead with the whole franchise company.

A strategic entertainment buyer would underwrite expected cash from characters, formats, catalog, consumer licenses and expansion options, then compare the price with relevant transactions and its own distribution economics.
EBITDA and discounted cash flow (today’s value of future cash) are useful for an established earning business; revenue multiples require a defensible profit conversion.
A sports operator may value the participation business separately.
Royalty relief answers the narrower question of value attributable to the brand asset; it is not a ceiling on the whole franchise.

detail.heading: Precedent: Peanuts (verified, with a currency correction)
items: WildBrain agreed to sell its 41% stake for C$630M (Canadian dollars).
Proportional arithmetic implies about C$1.54B for 100% of the equity — not US$1.54B, and not automatically enterprise value.
WildBrain disclosed C$27M fiscal-2025 EBITDA directly attributable to that stake: 630 / 27 = about 23.3×.
Its C$43M recognized figure includes consolidation benefits and is a different denominator.
The issuer’s transaction presentation labels the multiple approximately 23×. The deal closed in March 2026 (Sony closing announcement).
This supports Claude’s point that mature franchises can attract premium pricing — but the multiple describes that deal’s attributable earnings, not a blanket EV/EBITDA quote for Carter.
Mechanical 23× test only: $5M attributable earnings → $115M; $10M → $230M; $25M → $575M; roughly $43.5M → $1B.
These are not Carter comparables adjusted for growth, concentration, capital needs, ownership or debt. The route to a premium is proving a repeatable franchise a buyer can expand efficiently.

detail.heading: Precedent: Roald Dahl (Netflix)
items: Validates the acquisition architecture: Netflix’s official announcement describes a story universe across films, television, publishing, games, immersive experiences, theatre and products, supported by more than 300M books in 63 languages.
The announcement does not disclose a purchase price.

Claude’s approximately 18× revenue figure should stay a reported/constructed comparison until the deal price and same-period company revenue are reconciled; dividing a US-dollar price by pound-denominated revenue is invalid.
Illustration: 18× revenue on Carter’s hypothetical $25M IP-company revenue = $450M. At a 20% EBITDA margin that is 90× EBITDA; even at 50% margin it is 36×.
The attractive headline hides the growth and profit expectations it requires. Use it as a demanding strategic test, not a baseline price for an unfinished library.

detail.heading: Answer to Claude’s question 7
items: An acquirer buying the whole Carter franchise would mainly value its future cash flows, business assets and synergies, cross-checking earnings and transaction multiples.
Brand royalty relief is useful for a separate brand valuation or purchase-price allocation.
Present the franchise price first, the component economics second, and the narrower brand calculation below.
Never add the trademark value to the same business’s transaction value.

detail.heading: The brand name alone: royalty-relief method
items: Royalty relief = today’s value of the after-tax royalties the business would otherwise pay to use the brand. Brand Finance describes this approach for its rankings.
Simplified formula: next-year eligible branded revenue × royalty rate × (1 − tax) ÷ (discount rate − growth).
Assumptions: 12% discount rate, 3% perpetual growth, 25% tax.
Royalty rates below are hypothetical test inputs, not established Carter or entertainment-sector benchmarks. Steady growth is an illustration, not a shortcut for valuing a startup.

detail.heading: Branded revenue needed for a $500M or $1B brand
What the brand table really means
items: At 5%, $2.4B eligible next-year revenue produces $120M pretax / $90M after-tax brand benefit, capitalized at 12% minus 3% to reach $1B.
If independent licensees generate that revenue, Carter’s royalty receipts would be $120M — not $2.4B of Carter company revenue.
Retail sales and operating net revenue must not be mixed in the same denominator.
Change the risk and the answer changes: at 5% royalty and 3% growth, a $1B asset needs $1.867B revenue at a 10% discount rate, or $3.2B at 15%. None is a current appraisal.
A larger discount rate may suit an unproved business; real forecasts need finite growth stages, failure risk and a defensible royalty range.
Timing: $1B reached ten years from now is about $322M today at a 12% discount rate, before interim cash flows.

Separate ten-year ramp ($25M → $500M annual eligible revenue, 5% royalty, 25% tax, 10% discount, 3% terminal growth): today’s brand value is about $157.4M. A future run-rate target is not today’s valuation.

Applying 5%/12%/3%/25% to the $300M franchise-company revenue gives a $125M brand asset — while the company could reach $1.02B under the separate 12× EBITDA assumption. A billion-dollar company announcement does not establish a billion-dollar trademark.

detail.heading: Verdict for Coach
items: Keep the billion-dollar ambition.
Build the franchise around repeatable stories, partner distribution and high-quality licensing.
Present it as a destination with measurable gates.
A billion-dollar standalone brand would need far wider economic use than one successful documentary or series.
The current evidence justifies pursuing the first proof; it does not establish a $500M or $1B valuation today.

detail.heading: Earnings hurdle at an illustrative 10× EBITDA (not a market price or ceiling)
Why the 11% column: FranklinCovey as a real-world yardstick
items: FranklinCovey reported fiscal 2026 revenue of $261.5 million and adjusted EBITDA of $28.9 million — about 11.1% [S31].
Its education division generated $76.2 million; Leader in Me reaches more than 8,000 schools worldwide.
This is an operating-scale reference, not a company valuation comparison. A modeled 20% margin is ambitious next to it.
At a purely illustrative $15,000 annual school contract, $250 million revenue would need roughly 16,667 school-equivalent contracts — or a broader mix of large revenue streams.
That requires an international sales and delivery organization, not just strong personal recognition. Higher pricing, corporate contracts and entertainment can change the mix; each needs proof.

detail.heading: A premium multiple changes the math, not the need for evidence
items: At an assumed 20× EBITDA, $500M needs $25M EBITDA and $1B needs $50M — at a 20% margin, $125M and $250M revenue.
At 5×, the earnings hurdle is four times as large.
None of these multiples is an offer or a demonstrated Carter comparable.
What a buyer pays depends on growth, durable contracts, customer concentration, key-person dependence (how much rests on Coach himself), library economics, strategic fit and market conditions.

A uniquely valuable franchise or audience can sometimes win a premium before mature earnings — but that needs credible future cash flows and competing buyers. Nostalgia alone does not establish the premium.
Build the evidence that improves bargaining power instead of picking whichever multiple produces a billion-dollar headline.

Copy the mechanism, not the multiple: fast feedback, repeat buyers, global distribution and reusable production capacity.
Carter’s reusable assets: characters, formats, story knowledge, production systems, audience relationships and qualified partners.
The company stays an entertainment/brand business that uses AI — not an AI company.
The test: does each hit make the next cheaper, easier to distribute or more valuable to license? If not, speed won’t build a franchise.

items: Higgsfield’s August 17, 2026 company release reports a $400M financing at a $5.4B valuation, with $700M annualized revenue that month.
That is billions, not a $5M valuation.

items: Fast feedback.
Repeat purchase.
Global distribution.
Reusable production capacity.
A product that improves as demand grows.

detail.heading: The investable question
items: Does the next successful release make the next one cheaper to produce, easier to distribute or more valuable to license?
If every title starts from zero and depends entirely on Coach’s time, production speed alone will not create a franchise premium.

items: We cannot calculate “money he lost” without historical offers, audience analytics, expenses, contracts, and decisions.

Use real basketball history as the source for refined warm-ups, jerseys, and outerwear. Let the archive inform shape and narrative, not a copied team mark.
Current FW26 assortment spans outerwear, varsity, knitwear, shorts, sports objects, hats, bags, and a baseball jersey, presenting a broad lifestyle system with multiple colorways and price levels.
Give each drop a name, lookbook, origin note, and complete outfit. Add a ball, bag, towel, journal, and cap so the Academy feels like a place and practice.
The 2026 report identifies a difficult, value-conscious market and pressure to improve product relevance and operating discipline. Inference: Academy should validate small batches before scaling.
Use deposits, waitlists, and numbered microdrops to test real conversion. Do not mistake attention or nostalgia for guaranteed sell-through.

The Lyst Index is a quarterly current-demand signal, not a permanent ranking. Older lists are stale. Inference: monitor current movement in branded sportswear, footwear, and cultural collaborations rather than copying an old winner.
Review quarterly search/engagement signals, then adjust color, category, and collaborations. Never present an old index as current proof of demand.

detail.heading: Four design rules
items: 1. Start with the court hero. The first recognizable Academy product should be a genuine 7-inch mesh basketball short, with a flat waistband, drawcord, lined body, side pockets, clean leg opening, and one controlled court-line graphic. The silhouette is the identity. A new logo on a generic short is not enough.

2. Build a coordinated wardrobe. The launch should read as one uniform: heavyweight tee, court short, reversible jersey or numbered practice top, zip warm-up, hoodie, cap, and premium ball. Academy should remain basketball-specific rather than borrowing the crests or codes of Louis Vuitton, Wales Bonner or ALD.

3. Use exact brand masters. The current identity is the supplied Coach Carter wordmark and supporting typography. There is no invented CC or CCA varsity mark in this direction. “Academy” can be a secondary descriptor, but must be set deliberately and must not be passed off as part of the official master logo.
Exact logo files are assets; they are not yet manufacturing-certified until they have vector/raster, color, size, and decoration specifications.

4. Let flash come from construction: contrast piping, satin or mesh, tonal court diagrams, reflective hits, chenille, embroidery, numbered editions, and precise gold accents. Use one primary mark, one basketball detail, and one intentional accent per garment.

detail.heading: The honest bottom line
detail.note: The opportunity is real enough to test because Coach Carter combines recognizable basketball language, a durable story, and a product category with existing wardrobe behavior. A billion-dollar brand valuation is a long-range outcome that would require repeatable content, licensed or owned extensions, distribution, material revenue, and audited operating performance. Fashion can be the visible front door, but it cannot be valued at that level from a mockup, a nostalgic audience, or a single sellout. The correct first move is a high-quality, measurable Academy uniform drop that earns the right to expand.
